cases.refreshed: Free. Registration Required. Please call (408) 350-3239 to set up a free one-on-one counseling appointment. Do you have questions about Medicare or Medi-Cal? Sourcewise's HICAP counselors offer one-on-one counseling for those looking to make an informed decision about their Medicare and Medi-Cal options. HICAP Counselors answer questions about: Original Medicare (Part A & B); Medicare Advantage Plans (Part C); Prescription Drug Coverage (Part D); Supplemental Insurance (Medigap); Limited Income Programs for Medicare; Medicare and Medi-Cal Options; Tips for Avoiding Medicare Fraud. Appointments are available in various languages upon request. ** HICAP Counselors do not sell or endorse and are not affiliated with any insurance companies. HICAP's goal is to inform and educate the community so that individuals can make an informed decision about their healthcare options. **

cases.refreshed: ESL Conversation Club continues at Cupertino Library this year. Please join us for this fun sharing experience. Improve your English listening and speaking skills and learn about other cultures in a supportive environment. This program is for adults aged 18 and older who speak basic English. *We will be holding ongoing weekly meetings in Room 201A on the second floor. Space is limited and online registration is required. Registration will open one week prior to each meeting. For accessibility accommodations (e.g., ASL), please fill out the online form at sccld.org/accessibility 7+ days prior to the event. If you need assistance with the form, speak with a staff member at your local library, call (408) 540-3945, or email us at ask@sccl.org.

cases.refreshed: Philosophy for Life: A friendly reading and discussion group at the library, exploring big ideas about how we live and what we value. Why do we believe that success means constant hustle, that more is always better, or that everyone must go it alone? What other ways of thinking might help us make sense of everyday life? Together, we'll read accessible texts from different philosophical traditions and enjoy open, respectful conversations about the assumptions shaping our world. Open to adults, young adults and seniors. No background in philosophy required—just curiosity and a willingness to talk and listen. We'll read the following books: Living for Pleasure: An Epicurean Guide to Life by Emily A. Austin; A Guide to the Good Life: The Ancient Art of Stoic Joy by William B. Irvine; Choosing Freedom: A Kantian Guide to Life by Karen Stohr; On Being and Becoming: an Existentialist Approach to Life by Jennifer Anna Gosetti-Ferencei; Blooming in the Ruins: How Mexican Philosophy Can Guide Us Toward the Good Life by Carlos Alberto Sánchez. We'll meet every first and third Sunday at the Rinconada Library from 3:30 PM to 4:45 PM. In order to ensure an engaging discussion in which all can participate, attendance is limited to registrants. If the maximum capacity has been reached, please join the waitlist and you will be notified if you have been added to the group. Also, if you need to cancel your registration, please do so by 6:00 PM the Thursday before the meeting so people on the waitlist can be registered. *A detailed list of readings for each meeting can be found on the library calendar under the date of the corresponding meeting. Moderated by Natalia & Lottie, PACL staff. For November 15th: Topic: An Epicurean in Public Life: Justice and Injustice "Justice's greatest reward is peace of mind." Fragment 80. "Justice was never an entity in itself. It is a kind of agreement not to harm or be harmed, made when men associate with each other at any time and in communities of any size whatsoever." Principal Doctrine 33. "Injustice is not an evil in itself. Its evil lies in the anxious fear that you will not elude those who have authority to punish such misdeeds." Principal Doctrine 34. "It is impossible to live the pleasant life without also living sensibly, nobly, and justly, and conversely it is impossible to live sensibly, nobly, and justly without living pleasantly. A person who does not have a pleasant life is not living sensibly, nobly, and justly, and conversely the person who does not have these virtues cannot live pleasantly." Principal Doctrine 5. Literature: Living for Pleasure. An Epicurean Guide to Life by Emily A. Austin. Ch. 8 (pp. 80-91). Some Questions to Discuss: Based on the ideas expressed in the Principal Doctrines, what is Epicurus's view on the source of justice in society? What is the connection that Epicurus draws between injustice and corrosive desires according to Austin's analysis of his views on injustice? Is it easy to be just? Is it hard to be unjust?

Moderated by Natalia & Lottie, PACL staff. For December 6th: Topic: Epicurus's Challenge to Our Society: Raising a Tranquil Child "The wise man will marry and beget children, as Epicurus tells us in Problems and his work On Nature; but he will marry according to his station in life, whatever it may be." Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, 10:119. "Natural wealth is limited and easily obtained; the riches of idle fancies go on forever." Principal Doctrine 15. "Some men spend their whole life furnishing for themselves the things proper to life without realizing that at our birth each of us was poured a moral brew to drink." Vatican Sayings 30. Literature: Living for Pleasure. An Epicurean Guide to Life by Emily A. Austin. Ch. 17 (pp. 180-190). Some Questions to Discuss: In our society, how realistic is Emily Austin's Epicurean plan for raising a child? What are possible impediments to the realization of her plan? What are possible solutions for overcoming these obstacles?

For December 20th: Topic: Becoming an Epicurean? "In other occupations, the reward comes with difficulty after their completion, but in philosophy delight coincides with knowledge. For we do not stand in need of the appearance of health but of true health." Vatican Sayings 54. "By love of true philosophy we are delivered from every disturbing and painful desire." Fragment 66. "The most important consequence of self-sufficiency is freedom." Vatican Sayings 77. "The impassive soul disturbs neither itself nor others." Vatican Sayings 79. Literature: Living for Pleasure. An Epicurean Guide to Life by Emily A. Austin. Chs. 23 (pp. 241-251) and 24 (pp. 252-266). Some Questions to Discuss: In your opinion, which of Epicurus's ideas, if any, have not lost their currency and would be beneficial to our society? What needs to be done to implement them? What challenges may their implementation face?

cases.refreshed: Stuck with a technology question? Need help with an ongoing issue or learning something new? Stop by the Rinconada branch library for our drop-in tech help Tuesday mornings. Staff is available to help with a variety of tech questions including: Learning to use Libby and/or Hoopla; Accessing library databases and services; Downloading and streaming content; Navigating the City of Palo Alto Library website; Downloading and using the new PACL app; Wi-Fi connection; Printing; Creating an email account; Basic computer skills; Installing and using common apps; And more… * Unfortunately, helping you fix damaged hardware or software is not within our scope. Help is given on a first-come, first-served basis. Please bring any devices you use, make sure they are charged, and have your necessary passwords. We look forward to helping you.
